source.title: Scale matters: Large language models with billions (rather than millions) of parameters better match neural representations of natural language
source.authors: Zhuoqiao Hong; Hao-Cheng Wang; Zaid Zada; H. Gazula; David Turner; Bobbi Aubrey; Leonard Niekerken; Werner K. Doyle; S. Devore; Patricia C. Dugan; Daniel Friedman; O. Devinsky; A. Flinker; U. Hasson; Samuel A. Nastase; Ariel Goldstein

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure and table captions are included, but plotted numeric values are not text-extracted; the body of Table 1 is also absent from the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scale-related downstream prediction in a new setting: predicting human ECoG responses from language-model representations. It does not test the original pretraining-loss or compute-allocation measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that perplexity on the podcast transcript decreases with model size, but it does not fit or test a power law for held-out pretraining loss. The encoding results concern ECoG prediction, not loss extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation. Layer-preference and lag findings do not measure a claim version. Comparisons with untrained SMALL, speech features and GloVe are controls/comparators, not scale-effect rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well LLM hidden-layer embeddings predict human ECoG signals through ridge encoding models. That is model-brain alignment, not the models' own downstream task performance or pretraining loss, so it is a related but different construct. Its one loss-like result, podcast-transcript perplexity falling with model size (Fig. 2A), comes from about 5,000 words across families with different data. It has no power-law fit and no numbers in the text, so it cannot bear on V1. Kaplan et al. is cited only to say the perplexity trend is consistent.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that larger LLMs, with lower perplexity, better predict ECoG responses, roughly logarithmically, across families and within GPT-Neo on a fixed corpus. Maximal encoding plateaus around 7B and declines for OPT-66B, which they attribute to the limited ~5,000-word stimulus. Peak-encoding layers shift relatively earlier with size, and optimal lags do not vary with size.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses hidden-layer representations and cross-validated ridge-regression encoding of ECoG responses to a podcast, rather than fitting held-out next-token loss against model parameters, tokens or compute. It does not fit loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Encoding performance varied with model size and brain region; the increase plateaued after MEDIUM for BA45 and TP, and OPT-66B declined. Ridge regression outperformed PCA plus OLS overall, though both showed a model-size relationship. The comparison also spans model families with different architectures and training corpora; GPT-Neo controls for training corpus within one family.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain-encoding correlation from LLM embeddings rises roughly logarithmically with model size (82M–70B, four families, and GPT-Neo on a fixed corpus). It plateaus near 7B, OPT-66B is significantly worse than some smaller models, and BA45 and TP plateau after MEDIUM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment of LLM representations with human neural responses to language improves logarithmically with model size, then saturates for the largest models on limited stimuli.

fits_no_version.finding: The best-encoding relative layer moves earlier as model size grows, a logarithmic trend across families (Fig. 4B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In larger LMs, the layers most predictive of brain activity sit relatively earlier in the network.

record.problems: The neural stimulus was one approximately 30-minute story of about 5,000 words, and the analysis used 160 selected electrodes from eight patients. Only the GPT-Neo family controls for training corpus across sizes; cross-family comparisons vary in architecture and corpus. Exact plotted values are not available in the extracted text. The authors note a plateau in neural encoding performance and a decline for OPT-66B.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were added for transcript perplexity because the paper does not fit a power law for held-out pretraining loss. Untrained SMALL and classic speech/GloVe comparisons were controls or comparators, not results of the scale effect. Layer-location results and the absence of significant lag variation do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss. Transcript perplexity is only described as decreasing with size, across families with different corpora.
No fixed-size shape comparison of loss.
Text LMs only; no other modality or training regime.
No downstream task performance of the models is measured; only brain-encoding correlation is reported.
No exponent fitting or comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link treats brain-encoding correlation as a downstream task. It is a representation-to-neural-signal alignment measure, so all rows are re-linked to none and the finding is moved to fits_no_version. The perplexity result (Fig. 2A) has no plotted values in the text and no fit, and rows_left_out declares it.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute; transcript perplexity is reported only as decreasing with model size.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict loss on larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal split is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
The study uses textual language models and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
The downstream evaluation is prediction of ECoG responses from language-model representations; other downstream tasks and performance as a function of pretraining loss are not tested.
No fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across counting, scheduling, data or fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT-2, GPT-Neo, OPT, and Llama 2 model families (cross-family comparison)
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained autoregressive language models; Llama 2 versions before RLHF
rows.operation_detail: Compared ECoG encoding performance across model sizes using hidden-layer embeddings and electrode-wise encoding models.

conditions.value: 10-fold cross-validation; maximum correlation across lags and layers, averaged across electrodes

rows.measure: Encoding performance: correlation between predicted and actual ECoG signals
rows.value: A logarithmic relationship was reported: larger models better predicted neural activity.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2B error bars represent standard error; exact values not stated in the text.
rows.locator: Results, “Larger language models better predict brain activity”; Figure 2B
rows.note: The cross-family result spans models with different architectures and training corpora. The reported metric is neural encoding performance, not held-out language-model loss.
rows.check: Measure is ECoG encoding correlation (brain alignment), not downstream task performance or loss. Cross-family comparison also confounds size with data and architecture.

rows.subject: GPT-2, GPT-Neo, OPT, and Llama 2 model families (cross-family comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximal ECoG encoding performance across model sizes.

conditions.value: Larger models, around and above 7 billion parameters

rows.locator: Results, “Larger language models better predict brain activity”; Figure 2B and Supplementary Figure 1
rows.note: The text describes a plateau in maximal encoding performance as model size increases.
rows.check: Plateau in brain-encoding correlation around 7B; a brain-alignment measure, not a V6 downstream task.

rows.subject: OPT-66B
rows.operation_detail: Compared the model’s maximum ECoG encoding performance with smaller models.
rows.baseline: Smaller models in the comparison; exact reference values not stated
rows.value: The OPT-66B model showed a decline in performance; it was significantly worse than some smaller models.
rows.uncertainty: Paired two-sided t-tests across electrodes, df = 159; exact p-values not stated.
rows.locator: Supplementary Figure 1 and author response to Reviewer 3
rows.note: The authors report that only OPT-66B was significantly worse than some smaller models after 13 billion parameters; they did not find conclusive evidence of decline for other model families.
rows.check: OPT-66B significantly worse than some smaller models in encoding correlation (Fig. S1, author response). This is brain alignment, not a claim version.

rows.subject: GPT-Neo SMALL and XL
rows.size_stated: SMALL: 125 million parameters; XL: 20 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoding performance across lags using each model’s optimal layer for each electrode.

conditions.value: −2,000 ms to 575 ms relative to word onset

rows.value: XL significantly outperformed SMALL for most lags in the stated range.
rows.uncertainty: Paired two-sided t-test across electrodes, df = 159, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected.
rows.locator: Supplementary Figure 3 and Results, layer-by-layer and lag-by-lag analysis
rows.note: The paper reports the outcome for most lags as an aggregate, rather than giving separate numerical values for each lag.
rows.check: XL vs SMALL encoding correlation across lags; a brain-alignment measure.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cross-family comparison across models from 82 million to 70 billion parameters; GPT-Neo XL versus SMALL across most tested lags
reader_labels.reason: The study reports a logarithmic increase in encoding performance with model size overall and significantly higher XL performance than SMALL for most tested lags (R1, R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Largest models and regional GPT-Neo comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The overall encoding trend plateaus around 7 billion parameters, OPT-66B declines, and regional increases are nominal and plateau after MEDIUM in BA45 and TP (R2, R3, R5–R9).
